turns.reply: Welcome, I'm glad you're here! Think about a fire or a heater on a cold day: what do you feel coming off it when you stand nearby?
Heat and light, yes. Some atoms give out something similar: tiny particles, called alpha particles, that a sheet of paper can stop. If you held paper in front of a source, what would reach your hand?

turns.student: the alpha particles would go through
turns.reply: Not quite. Paper is like a wall to alpha particles: they are stopped by it, so nothing gets through to your hand. Think of throwing a ball at a closed door. If you held a sheet of paper in front of an alpha source, what would your hand feel?

Yes, nothing reaches your hand: paper stops alpha. Even so, alpha is called ionising radiation, meaning it knocks tiny electrons off the atoms it hits. What do you think happens to an atom that loses an electron?
Yes, an atom that loses an electron becomes charged, and that's what ionising means. If a source has an activity of 50 Bq, how many of its atoms decay each second?

Activity just means how fast a source is decaying, meaning how many of its unstable atoms give out radiation each second. It's like a speedometer reading, but for decays. It's measured in becquerels (Bq), and 1 Bq means one decay each second. So if a source has an activity of 50 Bq, how many of its atoms decay each second?
This bit is a tricky one, so no worries. Do you want me to just tell you the rest of this one?

So, the answer is 50 atoms each second. Some nuclei are unstable and give out radiation to become more stable, called radioactive decay, and it's random. A Geiger-Muller tube counts decays, and the count rate is the number it records each second. The radiation can be alpha, beta, gamma or a neutron. An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so the nucleus loses 4 from its mass number and 2 from its atomic number, becoming a new element. Alpha is stopped by paper or a few cm of air, is highly ionising, and is most dangerous if swallowed or breathed in.

Next is beta radiation, which is a fast-moving electron given out by the nucleus when a neutron turns into a proton. A neutron has no charge and a proton has a positive charge. If a nucleus gains a proton, what happens to its atomic number?
recap: Alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper, so nothing gets through.
Ionising means the radiation knocks electrons off atoms, leaving them charged.
Activity is how many unstable atoms decay each second, measured in becquerels (Bq).
So 50 Bq means 50 decays every second.

turns.reply: Fair enough, I'll keep it short. Beta radiation is a fast electron fired out of the nucleus when a neutron turns into a proton. The nucleus now has one extra proton. What happens to its atomic number?
Not quite: it goes up by 1, because the nucleus gains a proton and the atomic number counts protons. If a nucleus has 6 protons before beta decay, how many does it have after?
Yes — 7 protons is right, because beta decay adds one. Gamma is different: it is energy sent out from the nucleus, with no mass and no charge. What stops gamma getting through, then?
recap: Beta radiation is a fast electron fired out of the nucleus.
It happens when a neutron turns into a proton.
The nucleus gains one proton, so its atomic number goes up by 1.
6 protons before beta decay means 7 protons after, a new element.
turns.diagramCaption: Paper stops alpha. A few millimetres of aluminium stop beta. Thick lead only reduces gamma.

turns.reply: Not quite: paper stops alpha, but gamma goes straight through it, and through your hand too. Only thick lead or thick concrete cuts it down. If gamma passes through your body that easily, what could it damage inside you?
Yes, cells and organs are right, since gamma passes through you and can damage DNA. If gamma has the most energy of all these waves, what might that mean for how well it passes through things?

turns.student: like more energy means it goes through stuff easier?
turns.reply: Now, radiation isn't only in labs: a little is always around you, even right now, from things like rocks and food. If it comes from rocks and food, what do you think makes it "natural" rather than man-made?
recap: Gamma is pure energy from the nucleus, with no mass and no charge.
Paper doesn't stop gamma, and it passes through your body too.
Only thick lead or thick concrete cuts gamma down.
Gamma can damage DNA inside cells and organs as it passes through.

turns.student: it's not made by people in labs?
turns.reply: A nuclear equation shows decay like a sum, with the mass numbers adding up the same on both sides. If a nucleus with mass number 226 gives off an alpha particle of mass number 4, what mass number is left?
So if one nucleus has mass number 226 and gives off an alpha particle with mass number 4, what mass number is left?

Yes, 222 is right: 226 take away 4 leaves 222. The radiation dose you receive is measured in sieverts (Sv), and 1000 millisieverts (mSv) make 1 sievert. If someone gets a dose of 2000 mSv, how many sieverts is that?
Yes, 2 sieverts is right: 2000 mSv divided by 1000 gives 2 Sv. That brings us to the end of this lesson. You answered questions on gamma radiation and on background radiation and nuclear equations.
recap: Background radiation is always around us, from natural sources like rocks and food.
A nuclear equation shows decay like a sum, with mass numbers matching on both sides.
Alpha decay: 226 minus the alpha particle's 4 leaves a nucleus with mass number 222.
Radiation dose is measured in sieverts, and 1000 mSv make 1 Sv, so 2000 mSv is 2 Sv.

turns.reply: Background radiation is the low level of radiation that is around us all the time, coming from things like rocks, the air and space. It's there everywhere, even when nothing special is going on.
